Test for chlamydia and gonorrhea with nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs). C
Suspect chlamydia or gonorrhea in patients with mucopurulent cervicitis, especially in women 24 years or younger. C
Consider doxycycline post-exposure prophylaxis in high risk persons (e.g. multiple partners, failure to use condom, transgender persons) expecially if a history of sexually transmitted infection.B

background.definition: Cervicitis is inflammation of the columnar epithelium of the endocervical canal and any area of columnar epithelium extending onto the ectocervix (ectropion). It is characterized by mucopurulent (yellow) endocervical discharge and/or endocervical bleeding induced by gentle passage of a cotton swab through the cervical os. See separate chapter on Pelvic Inflammatory Disease.

list.listitem: C. trachomatis infection is the most frequently reported infectious disease in the United States. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention 2015 data:
Overall incidence: 645.5/100,000 women/year in 2015; which is about twice the rate found among men (335.4/100,000)
Adolescent females (ages 15-19 years): 3485.2/100,000/year
Young women (ages of 20-24 years): 3630/100,000/year
Gonorrhea is the second most frequently reported infectious disease in the United States:
All women: 107.2/100,000/year in 2015
Adolescent females: 442.2/100,000/year
Young women: 546.9/100,000/year
Chlamydia prevalence in persons 14 to 39 years is 1.5% (95% CI 1.2%, 1.9%; 2011-2012 data). Prevalence rate in 2009 was highest in teens and young women.
Females between the ages of 15 and 24 years at family planning clinics: 6.3% (range 3.0%-20.3%)
Females younger than 20 years entering adult corrections facilities: 19.1%
The prevalence of gonorrhea was also highest in teens and young women in 2009:
Females (ages 15-20 years) in family planning clinics: 1.0%
Prenatal clinics: 0.9%
Females entering juvenile correctional facilities: 4.7%
In 1994, the cost of untreated chlamydial infections and their complications was $2 billion in the United States.
Chlamydia and gonorrhea cause pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), which may lead to ectopic pregnancy, infertility, and chronic pelvic pain.
Both infections may facilitate HIV transmission.

Both cause complications in pregnancy and childbirth, including chorioamnionitis, premature rupture of membrane, preterm labor, miscarriage, low birth weight infant, infant mortality, postpartum infections, and newborn infections.
C. trachomatis.
Neisseria gonorrhoeae.
Herpes simplex virus (especially HSV-2).
A high density of ureaplasma cultured from the cervix may be associated with non-specific cervicitis.
In most cases of cervicitis, no infectious cause is found. Other causes may be bacterial vaginosis, Mycoplasma (M.) genitalium, douching, and chemical irritants.

The pathogenic role of M. genitalium is less certain in women than in men. M. genitalium is detected in 10% to 30% of women with clinical cervicitis and the organism is more common among women with cervicitis than those without cervicitis according to the CDC.
C. trachomatis is a gram-negative intracellular bacterium that infects the columnar epithelium of the cervix, urethra, and rectum, as well as nongenital sites.

N. gonorrhoeae is a gram-negative diplococcus that grows and multiplies in the cervix, urethra, fallopian tubes, mouth, throat, eyes, and anus and can spread to sites distant from the primary site of infection.

Both infections are readily passed through sexual intercourse. Transmission is somewhat more likely from female to male than from male to female based on a systematic review of 7 studies with 752 couples.

In one study of 473 Louisiana women at low risk for acquiring STIs, there were significant increases in leukocyte infiltrates among subjects with monoinfections with M. genitalium (1.5% of the women) or C. trachomatis (2.1% of the women) compared to women with no detectable STIs.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Prior history of sexually transmitted disease (STD) (chlamydia, gonorrhea)
New or multiple sex partners (chlamydia, gonorrhea)

list.listitem: Screen for chlamydia in all sexually-active women 24 years or 25 years and younger and other asymptomatic women at increased risk, A including pregnant women. B
Screen for gonorrhea in all sexually-active women, including those who are pregnant, if they are young or have other population risk factors. B
The USPSTF recommends intensive behavioral counseling for all sexually-active adolescents and for adults who are at increased risk for STIs. B

Consider doxycycline post-exposure prophylaxis in high risk persons (e.g. men who have sex with men, multiple partners, failure to use condom, transgender persons) expecially if a history of sexually transmitted infection.B
Screen for chlamydia and gonorrhea in all sexually-active women 24 or 25 years and younger and other asymptomatic women at increased risk, annually.
Screen for chlamydia all pregnant women 24 years and younger and other pregnant women at increased risk.
In a high-risk population (prevalence 9.4%), offering a chlamydia test to all women would prevent PID with an NNS of 60.

Highly specific tests for chlamydia in women include cervical or urine strand displacement amplification, transcription-mediated amplification, and polymerase chain reaction (PCR), and the Chlamydia Rapid Test (Diagnostic Dev't Unit, Univ of Cambridge).

The optimal interval for chlamydia screening is uncertain. Risk factors should be taken into account. Rescreening at 6 to 12 months those women previously infected is appropriate because of high rates of reinfection. The optimal timing of screening in pregnancy is uncertain.

The optimal interval for gonorrhea screening in the nonpregnant population is not known. For pregnant patients with risk factors, screening is recommended at the first prenatal visit. A second screening should be done during the third trimester for those who are at continued risk or who acquire a new risk factor.

Male condoms made of latex or synthetic material reduce the risk of transmission of sexually-transmitted infections (STIs) including gonorrhea, chlamydia, and trichomoniasis. Predictors of adolescent reported condom use include condom use at first sex, intention to use a condom, and communication about condoms with a partner, but not knowledge about safe sex.

Brief educational interventions reduce condom use errors and may improve use of condoms among young black men attending STI clinics. Based on two systematic reviews of 31 studies, brief counseling interventions have some effect in reducing and preventing STIs, with high-intensity interventions most likely to show a benefit at 6 months or less. In a meta-analysis of 12 studies, new media interventions containing an interactive component are the most successful for improving condom use and intervention duration influences STI testing.

Consider doxycycline post-exposure prophylaxis in high risk persons (e.g. men who have sex with men [MSM], multiple partners, failure to use condom, transgender persons) expecially if a history of sexually transmitted infection. In the DoxyPEP trial 592 high-risk persons (MSM and trans women) were randomized to doxycycline 100 mg 24-72 hours after condomless sex or usual care. DoxyPEP reduced the risk of STI (12% vs 30.5%, p < .001, NNT = 5).

In a trial in Kenya, cis-gender women were randomized to doxycycline PEP after condomless sex or usual care. There was no significant difference in subsequent STIs (35 vs 50 infections, RR .73, 95% CI 0.47 to 1.13).
A meta-analysis identified 4 randomized trials of doxy-PEP with 1727 participants, mostly MSM. It was effeective at reducing the risk of chlamydia (RR .35, 95% CI .15 to .82) but not gonorrhea.
Natural membrane condoms are not recommended for protection against STIs. Female condoms may prevent STI transmission but evidence is limited.
There is fair evidence that use of the contraceptive diaphragm protects against gonorrhea, chlamydia, and trichomonas infections.
Antibiotic prophylaxis at the time of first trimester surgical abortion can prevent post-abortion upper genital tract infection; in this review, no regiment appeared best.
Risk reduction counseling for adults at the time of HIV testing does not reduce the risk of acquiring subsequent STIs.

Suspect chlamydia or gonorrhoea in patients with mucopurulent cervicitis, especially in women 24 years or younger, or when sustained endocervical bleeding is easily induced by gentle passage of a cotton swab through the cervical os. C
Test for C. trachomatis and N. gonorrhoeae infection using the most sensitive and specific test available (NAAT). C
Assess for signs of PID, and evaluate for bacterial vaginosis and trichomoniasis. C

In many cases, especially among women over age 30 years or in persistent cases, no organism is identified. Consider factors such as exposure to a chemical irritant (e.g., douching) or idiopathic inflammation in the zone of ectopy. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Mucopurulent endocervical discharge in a young woman
Yellow-green malodorous vaginal discharge; trichomonads on vaginal saline prep
Thin white malodorous vaginal discharge; clue cells on vaginal saline prep; few WBCs
Pelvic pain; uterine, adnexal, or cervical motion tenderness

list.listitem: Purulent endocervical discharge with edema, erythema, or easily induced bleeding with a cottom swab suggests chlamydial or gonococcal infection.

Opaque endocervical discharge or easily induced bleeding alone are both about 42% sensitive; the presence of 2 or more of these signs is quite specific for chlamydia cervicitis. These signs are more likely to predict infection in young women.
Assess for signs of PID (see Differential Diagnosis section).
Signs of cervicitis may be absent despite chlamydial or gonococcal infection.

In a study of 288 adolescent women presenting to an urban ED with vaginal discharge or lower abdominal pain, 27% were diagnosed with trichomonas, chlamydia, or gonorrhea. The history alone was only 55% sensitive and 60% specific; adding a pelvic exam did not improve diagnostic accuracy. Clinicians should have a high index of suspicion and a low threshold for ordering urinary tests for infection.
Test for chlamydia with a NAAT.
Test for gonorrhea by culture, NAAT, or nucleic acid hybridization test. NAATs are more sensitive than culture.
When an STI is suspected, a patient administered vaginal PCR swab is also highly specific and quite sensitive for chlamydia or gonorrhea (LR+ 91 and LR− 0.09).
NAAT of urine, urethral, vaginal, and cervical swabs or via endometrial biopsies can also be used to detect M. genitalium. NAAT diagnosis should be followed with an assay for macrolide resistance.
Evaluate for bacterial vaginosis and trichomoniasis with a wet prep of vaginal secretions.
Leukorrhea (increased numbers of WBCs on saline prep of vaginal secretions) in the absence of inflammatory vaginitis is associated with chlamydial and gonorrheal cervicitis.
Screening for gonorrhea and chlamydia can be done using a NAAT on urine. This may be the most cost-effective screening method if a pelvic examination is not otherwise needed.

A point-of-care test that simultaneously tests for C trachomatis, N gonorrhoeae, and trichomonas (Visby Medical Sexual Health Test) had excellent sensitivity (97.4%-99.2%) and specificity (96.9%-99.4%) for all 3 pathogens.
See the algorithm in for an approach to the evaluation of the patient with suspected cervicitis.
If any organism-specific test is positive, treat with one of the CDC-recommended regimens described below.A
First-line treatments for cervicitis are azithromycin 1 gm orally in a single dose or doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 7 days.A
When treating a gonococcal infection, treat also for chlamydia unless a NAAT for chlamydia is known to be negative.C
Test of cure to detect therapeutic failure is not recommended unless adherence is in question. C
For undifferentiated cervicitis, first-line therapy based on CDC guidelines (2021) is doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 7 days. The alternative is azithromycin 1 gram in a single dose.
Any positive organism-specific test for C. trachomatis or N. gonorrhoeae is an indication for drug treatment.

Dispensing a doxycycline kit in the ED following diagnosis was associated with an increased likelihood of completing treatment in a before-after quasi-experimental trial (69% vs 46%, p = .002, NNT = 4).
Test of cure is not recommended unless adherence is in question.
See also separate chapter on Pelvic Inflammatory Disease.

Treat presumptively for chlamydia in high-risk patients with cervicitis. This is especially important if follow-up is not ensured or if a less sensitive test is used. Treat cervicitis presumptively for gonorrhea if the prevalence is high (>5%) in the clinical population.

CDC guidelines (2021) recommend treatment treating C. trachomatis infection with doxycycline 100 mg orally twice per day for 7 days (98% cure rate). Recommended alternatives are azithromycin 1 gram orally in a single dose or levofloxacin 500 mg orally once daily for 7 days.
During pregnancy azithromycin 1 gm orally in a single dose is recommended, with amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily for 7 days as the alternative.
In neonates, erythromycin base or ethyl succinate 50 mg/kg/day orally divided 4 times daily for 14 days is recommended.

For adults and adolescents, ceftriaxone 500 mg IM in a single dose for persons weighing less than 150 kg (330 lbs) is recommended. For persons weighing more than 150 kg, 1 gram is recommended. If chlamydia has not been excluded, treat as above for chlamydia with doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days as the first choice.
Alternative regimens for gonorrhea include gentamicin 240 mg IM single dose plus azithromycin 2 gm orally single dose or cefixime 800 mg orally in a single dose.

Neisseria gonorrhoeae antimicrobial resistance to ciprofloxacin, penicillin, and tetracycline and elevated minimum inhibitory concentrations to ceftriaxone and azithromycin were found in isolates from men who have sex with men compared with men who have sex exclusively with women.
CDC guideline (2021) recommendations are based opn whether the organism is likely to be macrolide sensitive.
If macrolide sensitive: Doxycycline 100 mg orally 2 times/day for 7 days, followed by azithromycin 1 g orally initial dose, followed by 500 mg orally once daily for 3 additional days (2.5 g total).
If macrolide resistant or resistance testing not available: Doxycycline 100 mg orally 2 times/day for 7 days followed by moxifloxacin 400 mg orally once daily for 7 days.
Be aware of state and local requirements for STI reporting.
Gonorrhea and chlamydia infections are reportable in all states.
Patients treated for chlamydia or gonorrhea are at high risk for reinfection and should be monitored by retesting at 3 months.
Test-of-cure is unnecessary except during pregnancy.
Test pregnant women treated for chlamydia 3 weeks after therapy is completed.
Treatment regimens for chlamydia are highly effective, and persistent symptoms are most likely due to reinfection or due to a cause other than chlamydial infection.

Spontaneous resolution of infection at enrollment after a positive chlamydia screening test occurred in 44 women (22%) in one study. Reinfection at follow-up was significantly lower in women who had spontaneous resolution of initial infection (4.5% vs. 19.9%) suggesting that treatment may attenuate protective immunity.
Evaluate by culture with antimicrobial sensitivity testing those patients who have infection that persists after treatment for gonorrhea.
Instruct patients with chlamydia or gonorrhea infections to refer their sex partners for testing and treatment.

Treat those who had sexual contact with the infected patient during the 60 days preceding symptom onset or diagnosis. The most recent sex partner should be tested and treated even if the time of last sexual contact was more than 60 days.
Consider patient-delivered partner therapy if concerns exist that sex partners will not seek treatment.
Except for pregnant women, test-of-cure is unnecessary.
Consider retesting for chlamydia and gonorrhea in 3 months due to the high incidence of reinfection.
Instruct patients treated for chlamydia to abstain from sexual intercourse for 7 days after single-dose therapy or until completion of a 7-day regimen.
Instruct patients treated for gonorrhea to abstain from sex until therapy is completed and they have no symptoms.
Instruct patients to abstain until sex partners are treated.
Advise patients treated for chlamydia or gonorrhea to be tested for other STIs.
Treat chlamydia infection during pregnancy with azithromycin 1 g orally in a single dose. A
Alternative regimen is amoxicillin 500 mg orally three times daily for 7 days.
Test for cure 3 weeks after completion of therapy for chlamydia during pregnancy.
Treat gonorrhea during pregnancy with ceftriaxone 500 mg in a single IM dose plus treatment for chlamydia if infection has not been excluded.

Examine vaginal saline prep; test for GC and Chlamydia. Trichomonads present?
Treat presumptively for Chlamydia. If follow-up is insecure or if a test other than NAAT is used.
Consider presumptive treatment for GC if the prevalence is high (>5%) in the patient's population.

Await results of GC and Chlamydia testing.
